Grand Forks County by the numbers

Grand Forks County ranks 3 of 5 North Dakota counties in this guide by population, at about 72,764 people in 33,736 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $244,200, the median home value sits 9% below the North Dakota county median for this guide. The North Dakota county median income is $79,273, and Grand Forks County reports $68,450. Owner-occupancy is 52%, so renters hold about 48% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1981, about 42 years ago.

What is Grand Forks County, North Dakota?

Grand Forks County is in eastern North Dakota, with the Red River forming its eastern border, and its county seat and largest city is Grand Forks. The Dakota Territory legislature created it on January 4, 1873, and county government was organized on March 2, 1875. Boundaries have been unchanged since 1883.

The county covers 1,439 square miles, mostly agricultural land outside the urban area, and slopes gently north and east. It had 73,170 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 74,501 for 2025, which makes it the third most populous county in the state.

Neighbors in North Dakota are Walsh, Traill, Steele and Nelson counties. Across the river are Marshall and Polk counties in Minnesota.

What places and landscapes make up the county?

Beyond the city of Grand Forks, the county includes small towns and farm townships, with Larimore and Northwood among the communities named in the school and township listings and Thompson also served by a school district. East Grand Forks, Minnesota, is a core city of the metro area but sits in another state and county.

The Forest River crosses the upper western part of the county. Turtle River State Park, Kellys Slough and Little Goose National Wildlife Refuges, and the Prairie Chicken State Game Management Area are listed among its protected lands. Fordville Dam, Larimore Dam and Smith Lakes are the reservoirs.

  • Urban property: values set by the City of Grand Forks Assessing Department
  • Rural and small town property: assessed with township and city assessors through the county
  • Mobile homes: handled through the county Tax Equalization Office

What does the economy look like for county property owners?

The county's economy blends farming with the education, health and defense jobs concentrated in the city. The University of North Dakota, Altru Health System and the Grand Forks Air Force Base are the three largest employers listed for Grand Forks, with Grand Forks Public Schools next.

Rural owners face a different tax picture than city owners because agricultural land follows its own valuation approach under state rules. Morton County's assessment page makes the same point, saying agricultural land is valued with a state agricultural valuation guide while homes are assessed at market value. Ask the county Tax Equalization Office which category your parcel falls into.

Which offices handle property tax in Grand Forks County?

The Tax Equalization Office values property with township and city assessors, the Treasurer bills and collects, and the Recorder keeps ownership records. All three are in the county building area at 151 South 4th Street, Grand Forks, ND 58201.

OfficeRoleContact
Tax Equalization OfficeUniform assessment, mobile home permits and statements701-780-8259 (director); mail to PO Box 5294, Grand Forks ND 58206-5294
County TreasurerBills and collects real estate tax701-780-8292; PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638
RecorderRecords documents affecting title701-780-8262; PO Box 5066

The county staff directory lists a Director of Tax Equalization, a Deputy Director, a Real Estate Assessor at 701-780-8245 and a Real Estate Tax Assistant at 701-780-8251. Staff change, so confirm the right extension when you call.

How do Grand Forks County property tax dates work?

Taxes are due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1, with a 5 percent discount for paying the full year by February 15. State law sets statements to be mailed by December 26.

StepDate
Valuation dateFebruary 1
City or township board of equalizationFirst 15 days of April
County board of equalizationFirst 10 days of June
State board of equalizationSecond Tuesday of August
Budget notices from the treasurerAugust 31
Statements postmarkedBy December 26
5% discount deadlineFebruary 15
Abatement applicationNovember 1 of the next year

If you split the year, the first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15. Under North Dakota Century Code section 57-20-01, a 3 percent penalty applies after March 1 and again on May 1, July 1 and October 15, and the second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

How can I look up a Grand Forks County parcel?

The county posts online search tools that cover both the county and the city. They include Vanguard house information searches for each, a Tyler iTax site for real estate and mobile home tax information, an ArcGIS parcel map, and iDoc for recorded documents.

  • Use iTax to see the current tax balance by address, owner name or property number
  • Use the Vanguard pages to see valuation details
  • Use iDoc to search recorded documents by grantor and grantee

The county's GIS page warns that the maps are for reference only and are not a legal description. Order a survey or title search if a boundary matters to your sale.

How do I challenge a Grand Forks County assessment?

Contact the assessor for your parcel first, then appeal to the local board in April and the county board in June. State law lets the State Board of Equalization reduce a value only if you appealed at both the local and county levels.

Each owner receives a written notice showing true and full value for the current and previous year. After the August state meeting, you can apply for abatement of the current year's assessment by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable. Forms are on the State Tax Commissioner's website.

A city property owner appeals through the city board, and written, phone or electronic appeals count as appearing in person.

What happens when Grand Forks County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid tax becomes a lien, and a parcel with taxes delinquent into the third year can be foreclosed by the county. The owner can stop that by paying all taxes, specials, interest, penalties and costs by October 1, following notice served by June 1.

The county posts a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien on its website, and the 2026 notice is listed there. Once a county takes a tax deed, the former owner may buy back before resale, subject to the board of county commissioners.

A tax foreclosure can wipe out a mortgage, since the tax lien has priority. That is why servicers often advance the tax on loans without escrow and add it to the balance.

How does selling in Grand Forks County work when tax is due?

The unpaid amount is normally paid from your sale proceeds at closing, and the Recorder then records the deed. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, so you pay recording fees only. The Recorder lists a $1.00 per page copy fee and $5.00 for the first page of a certified copy.

If you inherited a house or fell behind, ask the Treasurer for the full payoff and ask the city or township about specials. A cash sale can close without a buyer's lender and appraisal, which removes one source of delay when a tax foreclosure date is near.

We buy Grand Forks County houses in any condition and handle the title company coordination, so the county balance is paid at closing.

More questions about Grand Forks County, ND Property Tax Guide

Where is the Grand Forks County Treasurer?

The Treasurer's mailing address is PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638, and the phone is 701-780-8292.

Who assesses property in Grand Forks County?

The Tax Equalization Office works with township and city assessors. The City of Grand Forks Assessing Department values property inside the city.

When is the discount deadline for Grand Forks County property tax?

February 15. Paying the full year by then earns a 5 percent discount, and the first installment is due March 1.

How many people live in Grand Forks County?

The 2020 census counted 73,170 people, and the 2025 estimate is 74,501.

Can I buy back a property after a county tax foreclosure?

Possibly. State law allows the former owner to repurchase before the county resells it, either in full or under an installment contract with the county commissioners.
